title: People turn down free money when the split feels unfair
body: In the ultimatum game, one player proposes how to divide a sum and the other can accept or reject; a rejection leaves both with nothing. Pure self-interest says the responder should take any amount above zero, since something beats nothing. In experiments since the first by Güth, Schmittberger and Schwarze in 1982, proposers typically offer about **40% of the pie**, and offers below roughly 30% are often rejected. Rejecting costs the responder real money, so the result shows that people will pay to punish what they see as unfair.

slides.question: Someone must split 10 coins with you; if you refuse, both get nothing. How many do proposers typically offer?
slides.explanation: About 4 in 10: proposers typically offer around 40% of the pie. Offers below roughly 3 in 10 are often rejected, leaving both players with nothing.

left.label: Self-interest says
left.text: Offer the smallest possible amount; the responder accepts, since something beats nothing.

right.label: People do
right.text: Proposers offer about 40%; responders often reject anything under roughly 30%.

slides.label: what proposers typically offer, in a 2004 review of 37 studies
slides.text: Among members of the same group, people often offer an even 50:50 split.

slides.heading: Do high stakes change it?
slides.text: In Indonesia, $30 offers were refused even though that equalled two weeks’ wages. But a 2011 study in India, with stakes of up to 40 weeks’ wages, found that as the stakes rise, rejection rates approach zero.

slides.question: Why do responders reject small offers, according to the two leading accounts?
options: They want to end the game fast
slides.explanation: One account calls rejection altruistic punishment, a lesson for the proposer; another calls it a failure to inhibit the urge to punish. Intoxicated players reject more, which supports the second.
